opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the report is interesting as a kind of exploratory catalog. The authors spent months poking at GPT-4 and documented some genuinely surprising behaviors: writing code, producing proofs in the style of Shakespeare, drawing unicorns in TikZ. Those are impressive, and I don't want to dismiss them.

But I'm quite skeptical of the framing. First, methodologically, it isn't really a scientific study. It's a collection of anecdotes, often cherry-picked successes, with no systematic evaluation, no control over whether the test items appeared in the training data, and no way for outside researchers to replicate anything since the model and its training corpus aren't open. When you test a system trained on a large fraction of the internet, you have to worry that what looks like reasoning is retrieval and interpolation from things it has effectively seen before.

Second, "AGI" is a term with no agreed definition, so claiming "sparks" of it is almost unfalsifiable. What I'd want to ask is: what are the specific cognitive capabilities, and how reliably does the system exhibit them? When you look at it that way, these models have some big gaps. They don't have a clear separation between linguistic competence and factual knowledge, so they confabulate. They don't maintain a persistent, updatable model of the world; you can't just tell them a fact and have it reliably integrated. They don't have good metacognition, meaning they don't know what they don't know, and their confidence isn't well calibrated. And their reasoning and planning are brittle. They'll solve a problem and then fail on a trivially perturbed version of it.

So my view is that large language models are a remarkable achievement, and they've shown that statistical learning over text captures far more than many of us expected. But I'd describe them as a powerful component, a kind of broad, shallow associative memory and language interface, rather than a general intelligence. Getting to something more robust will require modular architectures: separate components for knowledge, for reasoning and planning, for episodic memory, and for monitoring their own competence. The "Sparks" paper, in a sense, distracts from that engineering agenda by suggesting we're closer to the destination than we are.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it's a very interesting document, and the examples in it are genuinely impressive. There's no question that GPT-4 can do things that I would not have predicted a few years ago. But I have some real concerns about the framing, and particularly about the word "AGI" in the title.

The core problem is that the report is essentially a collection of anecdotes. The authors are very upfront that this is not a systematic evaluation. They tried things, they saw surprising behavior, and they wrote it up. That's fine as exploratory work, but it's not how you establish a scientific claim. When you have a system trained on essentially the entire internet, you can't rule out that it has seen something very close to the task you're testing it on. And when you're the one choosing the prompts and deciding which outputs to report, there's a natural tendency to find the examples that confirm what you're excited about. So I'd want to see held-out evaluations, controlled comparisons, and some accounting for what might be in the training data before I'd put much weight on any particular claim of a novel capability.

The second issue is the definition of general intelligence they're working from. They borrow a definition that lists things like reasoning, planning, problem solving, abstract thinking, learning from experience. And then they go through and sort of check off boxes. But if you look carefully, several of those boxes don't actually get checked. The model doesn't learn from experience in any ongoing sense. It doesn't have persistent memory. Its planning is quite weak, and the report itself acknowledges that. It can't really verify its own outputs. So even by their own criteria, it falls short on some of the things I'd consider most central to intelligence.

I'd also push back a bit on the idea that language fluency is evidence of general intelligence. These systems have become extremely good at producing text that looks like what a knowledgeable person would write. But we have a long history in AI of being fooled by that, going back to ELIZA. The model is, at bottom, learning a statistical model of language, and language encodes a tremendous amount of human knowledge, so it's not surprising that it can reproduce a lot of that knowledge and even recombine it in useful ways. Whether that constitutes "understanding" in a deeper sense, or whether it's a very sophisticated form of interpolation, I think is still open, and the report doesn't really settle it.

And then there's the practical side. These systems confabulate. They produce confident falsehoods, and they have no reliable way of knowing when they don't know something. A system that can't tell you when it's uncertain is, to my mind, not something I'd call generally intelligent, regardless of how well it does on a bar exam. That's not a minor rough edge, it's a fundamental architectural limitation of the approach as it currently stands.

So my overall assessment is that the report is valuable as a description of what the system can do, and the authors deserve credit for being honest about the methodological limitations. But I think the AGI framing does a disservice. It invites people to read more into these results than the evidence supports, and it tends to shut down the more important conversation, which is what exactly are these systems good at, where do they fail, and how do we build systems that are reliable enough to actually deploy for consequential tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate two questions: Does GPT-4 exhibit an impressive breadth of capabilities? Clearly it does. Does that establish that it has artificial general intelligence? I don’t think so.

One difficulty is that we don’t have an agreed-upon operational definition of AGI. If you show a system doing a collection of surprising tasks, that’s interesting evidence about its capabilities, but it isn’t necessarily a test of general intelligence. You also need to understand where it fails, how sensitive it is to the way you ask the question, and whether its successes hold up under systematic testing.

I would view “sparks” as a hypothesis-generating description. These systems give us plenty of phenomena to investigate. But I’d like to see the claims turned into controlled, reproducible experiments, with explicit criteria for what would count as evidence against them. The impressive examples are a starting point for that investigation, rather than a conclusion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish impressive performance from evidence of general intelligence. GPT-4 can do a remarkable range of things, and examples of those capabilities are worth studying. But a collection of interesting examples doesn’t establish AGI.

One difficulty is that we don’t know exactly what was in the training data. So when it solves a problem, it’s hard to determine how much genuinely new reasoning was required. Another is that these systems can succeed on a fairly sophisticated task and then fail on a simple variation. We need systematic tests that explore those variations, rather than focusing only on successful demonstrations.

To me, the important questions are: Under what conditions does it work? Where does it fail? Can it recognize when it doesn’t know? The report raises interesting questions, but I wouldn’t take it as establishing that GPT-4 has general intelligence.
